The Huns were a nomadic people who originated in the steppes of Central Asia and migrated westward, becoming renowned as expert cavalry warriors whose superior mobility revolutionized military tactics. Under Attila, they unified the fragmented Hunnic tribes and built an empire spanning from the Rhine all the way to Central Asia, extracting tribute from both the Eastern and Western Roman empires. His military campaigns were devastating. In 378, Hunnic influence on Germanic migration patterns became evident at the Battle of Adrianople, though it was primarily Gothic forces employed against Rome. More directly, Attila invaded Gaul in 451 but was defeated by a rare unified Roman response—a coalition of Romano-Frankish and Visigothic forces at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains. He sacked many Roman cities and demanded ruinous tribute that hastened the financial and military collapse of the Western Empire. The Huns also held Germanic peoples as tributaries and vassals, controlling the Ostrogoths and influencing the migrations of Visigoths and other groups. But their dominance proved fragile. After Attila's death in 453, his empire fragmented rapidly. Within decades, the Huns ceased to be a major historical force entirely, absorbed or displaced by the Germanic successor kingdoms they had once dominated.
